          Gemini's audit is a second opinion, not proof either. Gemini judged style patterns in this text — word choice, grammar, spelling and punctuation habits, and how closely the writing matches known AI and human patterns. It did not witness the writing, it can be inconsistent between runs, and it shares the known detector weaknesses: formal, polished, translated or non-native-English writing reads more AI-like to it, and AI text that was edited or humanized reads less. Never use this audit alone to accuse, grade, reject, hire or publish a claim about authorship.

          Honest note on these signals: the “everyday glue words” bar is a function-word share — a rough proxy for predictability, not perplexity — and this checker runs no language model. “Sentence evenness” is a sentence-length-variation proxy for burstiness, not the measurement a trained detector makes. Uniform sentences and formal vocabulary are associated with AI-like text, but formal human writing shares both — every one of these is a weak signal on its own, which is why the split also weighs the human touches (contractions, specifics, irregular rhythm) that separate plain AI output from AI text a person or a humanizer reworked.

          Stock phrases found

          Predictable / formal vocabulary found

          Counts are occurrences in this text only. These are style resemblance observations — common in AI-generated writing, and common in formal human writing too. No single word or phrase proves who wrote anything.

          Readability — separate from the resemblance score

          Revise this draft yourself

          Edit the draft by hand, in your own words. Nothing here rewrites the text for you. Work through this short list from the research saved below:

          • Add a specific example or reference only you would pick — a real detail, name, number or source you have checked.
          • Add your own judgment or critique — what you agree or disagree with, and why.
          • Vary sentence length and openings — mix short and long sentences; do not let every sentence start the same way.
          • Remove stock phrases — cut formulaic lines like “in conclusion” or “it is important to note” and say the thing plainly.
          • Simplify the meaning, not just the words — if a sentence is vague, decide what it actually claims and write that.

          0 words in this draft

          Disclosure reminder: if AI helped draft the original, disclose that help wherever your reader, school, employer or publisher requires it. Do not submit AI-written text as your own unaided work. Editing a draft yourself improves the writing — it does not change who or what produced the first version, and it is not a way around a rule.

          How this works — and why no detector can prove authorship

          What is measured. Detectors like ZeroGPT and QuillBot score statistical patterns, mainly predictability and uniformity. This checker measures the same family of signals openly, in your browser: sentence-length evenness (burstiness), stock AI phrases, formal report-style vocabulary, the share of everyday glue words (generated prose packs in more content words and fewer glue words than human prose), repeated phrases and openers, and average word length — then shows you each measurement instead of hiding it inside one verdict. Each sentence is then read two ways at once: how strong its AI-like signals are, and how many human touches it carries — true contractions, concrete specifics like names and numbers, questions or exclamations, irregular length. Strong signals with few touches read as AI-generated; signals mixed with touches read as AI-refined / humanized; weak signals read as human-typed. That second reading is what separates plain AI output from reworked AI text — an earlier version scored sentences on AI-like signals alone and filed most plain AI prose under “refined”, because smooth-but-unremarkable sentences landed in its middle band.

          Calibration, not training. On 4 Nov 2026 the scoring was rebuilt (heuristic v3) and tested against 26 texts: the five text types — paragraphs, formal essays, news articles, short and long descriptions, and casual chat / conversation — in human-written, AI-generated and humanized variants, the three built-in samples, and deliberate traps: a formal human essay, a formal human museum description, and a polite human business email full of stock formulas (the classic false positives), plus a humanized news report and a casual-toned AI blog post. The previous rules failed exactly the way users reported: a plain AI essay scored 0% AI-generated / 18% refined / 82% human, and a plain AI paragraph 0 / 28 / 72, because the sentence score rewarded stock phrases almost exclusively and its middle band swallowed everything smooth. The rebuilt signals and thresholds were adjusted until every plain AI text in the set came out AI-generated-dominant (paragraphs and essays at or near 100% AI-generated style, news 55–86%, descriptions 91–100%), every human text — including the formal traps — stayed human-dominant with 0% AI-generated, and the humanized paragraph, essay and description landed in between with the AI-refined share largest or near-largest. Two cases stayed weak, and they are named rather than hidden: casual chat / assistant-style replies and thoroughly humanized or casually rewritten text (a humanized news report, a casual AI blog post) still read mostly human-typed — their sentence patterns genuinely overlap human casual writing, and no threshold separated them without flagging real human chat and formal human writing instead. That was calibration of the in-browser rules on test texts written for the purpose — no model was trained, the test set was small and self-made, and no accuracy figure is claimed from it.

          Why the percentages are labelled “style”. Independent tests keep finding the same failures: ZeroGPT claims about 98% accuracy, yet independent tests put it nearer 70–85% and it scored a known human Lewis Carroll passage at 99.6% AI. QuillBot claims 99% “per RAID”, while independent 2026 tests put it nearer 70–78% — and its own humanizer beats its own detector. A widely shared test of 30+ detectors did not test ZeroGPT at all, and its QuillBot summary (98–100%) contradicts its own longer review (88% free, 78% Premium). Research consensus: detectors detect patterns, not authorship — formal, simple, translated and non-native writing gets flagged (in one Stanford study, 61.3% of non-native TOEFL essays were falsely flagged on average), while edited or humanized AI text slips through.

          The optional Gemini deep audit. If you tick “Deep audit with Gemini” and press its button, the same text is sent to Google Gemini with the key saved in your browser, under a forensic brief: read it word by word, then audit word choice, grammar, spelling and punctuation in separate passes, weigh the AI writing patterns against the human ones, and return its own three-way split with a reason for every sentence. That is a genuinely different second look — a language model can notice tone shifts, paraphrase seams and unnatural word choices that counting statistics miss. It is not a better class of evidence, though: Gemini is itself a language model, it can give different answers on different runs, it shares the false-positive problem on formal and non-native writing, and humanized text fools it too. That is why its result is always shown separately from the on-device result, never merged into one number, with the gap between them stated plainly.

          So what is this tool for? A quick, private, free second look: spotting passages that read as stiff or generic, checking your own drafts before you publish, and learning which patterns make text look machine-written. The on-device check never sends your text anywhere — only the optional Gemini audit does, and only when you ask it to. There is no account and no limit on the on-device check — and no accuracy claim, because an honest one cannot be made.

          Winston AI — what the research actually found (checked 4 Nov 2026). Two YouTube videos prompted a closer look at Winston AI: “I Tried the Best AI Detectors and Found the Most Accurate One” and the Short “TOP 10 FREE AI DETECTION TOOLS YOU SHOULD KNOW IN 2026”. Honest limits first: neither video could be verified — no transcript, captions, channel, date, length, test text or score could be retrieved for either, so neither is evidence that Winston was tested, and the Short's “free” framing is misleading for Winston, which has no ongoing free plan — only a 14-day trial with 2,000 credits (Winston pricing page, retrieved 4 Nov 2026). The one line in the Short that holds up is its own warning: a detector score is not proof of authorship, detectors disagree, and false positives and negatives happen.

          What Winston is. A paid, account-required, server-side product — the opposite shape from this free, no-login, in-browser checker. It shows a 0–100% Human Score and a five-band sentence Prediction Map (0–20 AI Generated, 20–40 Likely AI, 40–60 Uncertain, 60–80 Mostly Human, 80–100 Human Written), with a 500-character minimum in the app, a separate Flesch-Kincaid readability score, and a plain-language Explain summary — the presentation ideas this checker borrows, in its own words and colours. Winston itself warns the map is less accurate than the overall score and ignores sentences under 60 characters. What it discloses about method is only the signal names — linguistic analysis (perplexity, burstiness), comparison with known AI texts — plus API flags for zero-width-space and homoglyph attacks; the classifier, weights, training data and thresholds are proprietary and undisclosed, so none of its model, accuracy figures, or per-sentence probabilities can be copied or claimed here, and this checker does not use Winston in any way.

          Winston claimWhat the evidence shows
          “99.98% accurate” (homepage lineage)A conditional, internal figure: in the internal Luka report it was the AI-side figure (99.74% overall, 10,000 internal texts), and in Winston's own Winston 5.0 evaluation it applied only to documents of 2,000+ characters (99.87% overall on 12,000 internal English documents). Source: Winston site & help pages, retrieved 4 Nov 2026.
          “#1 on RAID”Two different things. The original peer-reviewed RAID benchmark (ACL 2024), at a fixed 5% false-positive rate, measured the older Winston version at 71.0% overall — behind Originality.ai (85.0%), ahead of GPTZero (66.5%) and ZeroGPT (65.5%) — and only 52.6% on paraphrased machine text. Winston's newer vendor-submitted RAID leaderboard figure (99.89% at a 1% false-positive rate) was not independently re-verified in this research. Both are reported with their version and false-positive rate, because neither erases the other.
          Price & accessPricing page retrieved 4 Nov 2026 (a 50% promotion was displayed, so live prices may differ — re-check on gowinston.ai/pricing): Essential $18/month standard ($9 promotional) with 100,000 credits/month, Advanced $29 ($14.50), Elite $49 ($24.50); AI detection costs 1 credit per word. Account and login are required for the app and the API. Language counts conflict by surface — 14 on the homepage feature list, 11 in its FAQ, 23 in the API docs — so no single count is quoted here.
          Detects humanized / paraphrased AIWeakly supported independently: RAID 2024 paraphrase accuracy was 52.6%, and one small 2026 hands-on test (Cybernews, 9 texts) detected lightly-edited AI only 11% of the time. Small tests are directional only — but they agree with the standing warning on this page: edited and humanized text scores lower on every detector.

          Open questions, stated plainly. The videos' sponsorship status is unknown; Winston's current live pricing and promotion were not verified live (all Winston figures above are page snapshots of 4 Nov 2026); the newer RAID leaderboard figure is vendor-reported; and no Winston-specific false-positive rate for non-native English writers was found — the class-wide warning stands regardless (Liang et al., Patterns 2023: seven detectors falsely flagged 61.22% of non-native TOEFL essays on average; Winston was not necessarily among the seven). What was borrowed for this checker is presentation and calibration only — banded scores with an Uncertain middle, sentence highlighting labelled as resemblance, readability shown separately, length gates, hidden-character flags, and a fixed limitations box. No rewrite-to-evade (“make it sound more human”) suggestions are offered here, deliberately.

          PapersOwl, GPTZero and Originality.ai — what the deeper research found (pages fetched 4 Nov 2026). A second research round read the three detectors the owner named, plus a screenshot of an Educraft guide to humanizing AI text. The headline is the same as Winston's, only stronger: none of the three can be copied, and none proves authorship — all three are proprietary classifiers whose weights, feature combinations and thresholds are undisclosed, and their headline figures (99–99.9%) are vendor-run numbers on clean, long, unedited AI text. Independent evidence is consistently lower: in the peer-reviewed RAID benchmark (ACL 2024, 6.29 million texts, measured at a fixed 5% false-positive rate) Originality.ai's then-current model came first at 85% overall and 96.7% on paraphrased text; Weber-Wulff et al. (2023, peer-reviewed) found no tool above 80%, collapsing to about 42% after light human editing and 26% after machine paraphrasing; Liang et al. (2023) found a mean 61.3% false-positive rate on human-written TOEFL essays by non-native writers. The honest standard is the vendors' own wording: Originality.ai 5.0 says a score “should be interpreted as a signal for review, not proof of authorship or misconduct”, and GPTZero says results “should not be used to punish or as the final verdict” — the wording this checker follows.

          Site (source)What is confirmed — and what is not
          PapersOwl (papersowl.com/ai-content-detector)Its page presents a free, no-account, unlimited classifier for students, English only, and gives no numeric accuracy, no architecture, no thresholds and no sentence-level method — only “highly accurate” and “billions of training data”, so there is no PapersOwl figure to adopt. Open question, stated plainly: the fetched page text mentions .doc/.docx/.txt upload and no word cap, but on a separate live visit the page showed a paste box only, a 10,000-character counter, no upload control, and the Analyze button returned no score for either of two sample texts — so its upload, its limit and its result format are unconfirmed either way. The 93.7% AI figure in its page text is sample content, not a scan result.
          GPTZero (gptzero.me)The most open of the three about method: it names perplexity, burstiness and style, says it moved to a deep-learning architecture in autumn 2023, and offers sentence-level highlighting — but its weights and thresholds are still undisclosed. Its stated minimum is 250 characters (about 50 words), the basis for the length gates here. Its vendor claims (99.9% on its home page) are not adopted: its RAID figure is reported inconsistently — 66.5% at a 5% false-positive rate in one compilation against 95.7% recall at a 1% false-positive rate in GPTZero's own framing — different operating points that cannot be compared directly. Open question: its pricing page rendered no prices at all when fetched on 4 Nov 2026, so no GPTZero price is quoted here.
          Originality.ai (originality.ai, pricing)Its product changed fundamentally in autumn 2026: the Lite, Turbo and Academic models were retired in September 2026, replaced by Originality 5.0 and 5.0 Max (October 2026), so older reporting about it is stale. Under 5.0 the score is the share of text in each class, not a confidence: Likely Original under 10% AI, Mixed Writing 10–80%, Likely AI 81–100%, with sentence highlighting and explanations. Pricing verified on its pricing page on 4 Nov 2026: Pro $14.95/month ($12.95/month billed annually) with 2,000 credits/month, Enterprise $179/month ($136.58/month billed annually) with 15,000 credits/month, and 1 credit = 100 words. Open questions: its free tier contradicts itself on the same page (100 credits one time vs 60 credits, 3 scans a day, renewing daily), so it is unconfirmed; and its scan app could not be checked without signing in, so nothing inside it is confirmed here. Its RAID result (85%) was earned by the retired 2.0 Standard model and says nothing directly about 5.0.
          Educraft humanization guide (owner's screenshot only)The article “How To Humanize AI-Generated Content in 5 Steps” by Theodosis Karagiorgakis could not be found live by title or author search, so its five steps are known only from the screenshot the owner sent and are marked as such: (1) custom instructions banning stock phrases and a long banned-word list, (2) custom assistants with reference files, (3) samples of your own writing, (4) making it personal — a defined audience and real experiences, (5) changing the pace — varying sentence length and structure. Its downloadable patterns guide could not be checked without giving an email, so its contents are unconfirmed. The steps are used here for one purpose only: they show why thoroughly humanized text reads as human-typed on style signals — which is a limit of every detector, never a feature of this one.

          Reading a result by text type — calibration. The same score means different things for different kinds of text, because humanizing edits move each type a different amount. This table is part of every reading, not fine print:

          Text typeHow to read the result
          Paragraph (about 50–150 words)Highly movable: varied rhythm and one personal detail can erase every measurable signal, and a single paragraph is close to too short for a meaningful style assessment — counts only, band held at Uncertain under 300 words.
          Essay (long, formal, edited)The text type most often misread in both directions: formal, heavily edited human essays already resemble AI style, and humanized AI essays converge on the same register. Never use an essay reading for an academic-integrity decision.
          News articleNews style is itself formulaic — neutral register, standard structure and transitions — so human and AI news copy overlap heavily. A resemblance reading only, with that overlap stated.
          Short description (about 30–100 words)Too short for rhythm statistics and dominated by stock phrases: below the length gate it is not assessable at all, and above it the reading carries a low-confidence flag. Never a confident band.
          Long description (300+ words)Length makes the counts steadier, but marketing copy is saturated with the exact stock vocabulary detectors key on — human marketers use it too — so expect human-written marketing copy to read AI-styled more often, and discount accordingly.
          Chat / conversationFragmentary, informal, short turns have no stable document rhythm to measure, and personal voice dominates. Individual chat turns are not scored meaningfully; a pasted conversation is read as one document with this warning attached — the known weakest case, named in the calibration record above.

          What was taken from this research — and what will never be copied. Taken, as presentation and honest signals only: sentence-level highlighting labelled as resemblance with the observation that caused each flag; the split reported as a share of text (a count), not a confidence; an explanation panel whose every reason is a visible count; length gates with uncertainty wording that widens as text gets shorter; descriptive stylometrics a browser can compute honestly — sentence-length mean, spread and range, disclosed stock-phrase counts, contrast-template and rule-of-three counts, transition-word load, em-dash density, repetition, and specificity counts (numbers, names, “I / we / you” pronouns) shown as raw counts, with the plain caveat that true perplexity cannot be measured without a language model; the calibration warnings above; “signal for review, not proof” beside every result; a plain-text report that is a description of what was measured, never a badge; and the anonymous, unlimited, no-login box itself. Never copied, deliberately: any vendor's proprietary code, weights or thresholds; any vendor accuracy claim (99%, 99.9%, 99.4%, 85%, 96.7%, 96.5%, a 1% false-positive rate) presented as this checker's accuracy; naming a generator (“written by GPT-4 / Claude / Gemini”) — no vendor evidences per-generator attribution; proof or certification badges, seals or “Verified Human” stamps; plagiarism, OCR or fact-checking features, which need external indexes a browser checker does not have; any humanizer feature; and any rewrite-to-pass coaching or promise of undetectability, in any form.

          What makes text read AI-like — the saved research

          What this is. A short, saved summary of the research read on 4 Nov 2026 into how AI text is reworked — six YouTube videos and one article about “humanizing” AI writing — kept here so the ideas behind this checker’s feature list stay visible. It describes observable style patterns and what detectors are said to watch. It is not a how-to for defeating a check, and nothing in it is a promise that any edit changes any detector’s verdict.

          Evidence limits — read first. No verbatim transcript was retrieved for any video: what is known comes from video descriptions, chapter lists and, for two videos, secondary AI summaries of them. Two sources could not be confirmed at all and their content is unknown, not researched fact: the video at youtube.com/watch?v=5JzgzZ7xBYI (nothing about it — title, channel, method — could be retrieved) and the EduCraft article “How to Humanize AI-Generated Content in 5 Steps” at educraft.tech (the page could not be opened and no copy was found, so its five steps are unknown and are not listed here). Detector figures quoted by the sources — “bypass every single time”, “100% to 0%”, “0% AI detection” — were asserted in descriptions, not demonstrated in any material that could be checked; the one retrieved figure pair (94% AI before a tool rewrite; 100% “unique” afterwards) came from secondary summaries and the second figure was a plagiarism score, not an AI-detection score.

          The 15 techniques, grouped by the signal each one targets

          Predictability — how guessable the next word is

          • Reconstruct from meaning — grasp the point, forget the original wording, rewrite it as your own explanation.
          • Remove stock phrases and overused transitions — cut “therefore / however / in conclusion” overuse and formulaic framing.
          • Train the model on your voice in advance — standing instructions, a custom assistant, samples of your own writing (pre-generation, not editing).
          • Tool rewrite / tool generation — a paraphraser or generator rewrites the text. Described by the research; deliberately not offered by this checker — see the line below.

          Uniformity — even sentence lengths and shapes

          • Vary sentence length deliberately — mix short and long sentences; break the metronome rhythm.
          • Vary sentence openings and syntax — different openings, inverted or combined sentences; never the same pattern twice in a row.
          • Break the default argument order — reorder ideas instead of following the model’s first logical sequence.

          Certainty and tone — absolute, flat, surface-level writing

          • Hedge where honesty requires it — “may”, “it appears”, “is likely” instead of absolutes the evidence does not support.
          • Simplify meaning and cut vagueness — keep the claim, drop the padding.

          Depth and specificity — facts without judgment or grounding

          • Add critique and interpretation — other viewpoints, limits, what you question and why.
          • Add specificity — concrete examples, data and references you have actually checked.
          • Personalise — your own experience and voice, where the format allows it.

          Process — where the words come from

          • Write the thinking yourself first — your notes and outline first; AI, if used at all, only selectively.
          • Check, revise, re-check — using a checker as revision feedback on your own draft.
          • Review and refine as a final human pass — read for meaning and flow before anything is submitted.

          Legitimate editing vs evasion — the clear line

          Legitimate editing is when the author owns the ideas, verifies the facts and citations, and discloses AI help as required by the reader, school, employer or publisher — the techniques above are then ordinary good writing. It becomes evasion when the same techniques are used to present model-written text as unaided work in order to defeat a check — when the detector score, not the writing, is the goal. This checker supports the first use only: it shows the patterns, and the revise helper leaves every edit to you.

          Contradictions in the research

          • Do rewriting tools work? The sources contradict each other: one says never use them (inaccurate, they damage quality), one teaches a manual method while also promoting them, and one uses a tool as its whole method. Unresolved — and every source had something to sell (services, courses, affiliate links or a tool offer).
          • Are word swaps enough? The sources broadly agree they are not: structure and thinking have to change, not just synonyms — and removing punctuation habits like em dashes is named as a trick that no longer works.
          • Does a “pass” generalise? The same researcher behind one video warns elsewhere that short passages checked in chunks can all read clean while the whole document is flagged — a pass on a paragraph does not carry to a full document.
          • Hedging vs simplifying pull opposite ways if applied crudely — more uncertainty language is not simpler writing — and no source retrieved explains how to balance them.

          Risks and limits

          • Meaning and facts drift. Rewriting — above all automatic rewriting — can flatten tone, change meaning and invent detail. Understand the sentence first, then rewrite it, and re-check every fact and citation.
          • Detectors change. The sources themselves say detectors keep getting stricter and old tricks stop working. Any score is tied to one tool, one version, one passage length.
          • Scores are not proof, in either direction. Formal, templated or non-native human writing can read AI-like; edited AI text can read human-like. A low score does not make undisclosed AI work compliant with any rule, and a high score does not prove misconduct.
          • “Unique” is not original. Rewriting someone else’s text until a similarity checker says 100% unique is still not your work — attribution and permission still apply.
          • The evidence is weak. Single, creator-chosen passages, no controls, no replication, commercial interests throughout — treat every effectiveness claim in this research as unproven.

          What this checker does with all of it: measures the observable features openly (see “Style features” in every result), labels everything style resemblance, not proof of authorship, and offers no rewriting, no humanizer and no score guarantee — deliberately.

            • Upload a photo, let Gemini analyse it, and get an SEO title, description and keywords — then strip the old metadata, embed the new one, and export ready-to-upload files and CSVs for every major stock platform.

            • Free and unlimited. No credits, no daily limits, no premium tier. Full-resolution downloads are always free here — including the transparent PNG from the Background Remover, the same download other sites charge for or downgrade. Our motto: premium features, unlimited use.

            Privacy

            • Free, with no account. MShop needs no sign-up and no login — you arrive and start working. There is no MShop account holding your details, because there is no account at all.

            • Everything runs in your browser. Every tool works on your own device. No photo is uploaded to an MShop server — MShop has no server receiving your files. The only file that ever leaves your device is the analysis copy you choose to send to Google’s Gemini when you run the Generator or Trend Hunter.

            • PDFs stay in your browser too. The PDF Compressor processes PDFs only in your browser — they are never uploaded to an MShop server.

            • Shared Tray photos stay in your browser. Tray photos are stored only in your own browser (IndexedDB, on your own device) — never on our server. They survive a reload, a closed tab and a new tab in the same browser and profile until you press Clear saved photos in the tray, clear this browser’s site data, or the browser evicts storage. They do not transfer to another browser or device. Use Pause browser saving in the tray any time to keep new photos only until reload — and if browser storage is unavailable, photos are simply kept only until reload while every tool keeps working.

            • Your Gemini key is yours alone. You enter your own key in the app — it is never asked for in chat and never baked into the page. It is stored only in your browser, with a session-only option that keeps it just until you close the tab. It is never sent to MShop, and it is sent only to Google, in a request header, when you run a generation.

            • History stays in your browser too. Generation History is saved locally in this browser only, with controls to reuse or delete entries — delete one, or clear your browser data and it is all gone. Nothing is sent anywhere else.

            • Downloads carry only the metadata you approve. When you embed and download, the file’s old metadata is stripped and replaced with only the new title, description, keywords and any rights fields you set — nothing else is written into the file.

            • Right-click blocking is a deterrent only. MShop blocks the right-click menu and the usual inspect / view-source shortcuts. That slows casual copying; it cannot make any web page’s code truly uncopyable, because your browser must receive the code to run it. We would rather say that plainly than oversell it — the real privacy protection above is that this page holds no secrets and your files never leave your browser except the copy you send to Gemini.

            • The Compressor, Background Remover, Watermark Remover and the other free tools need no Gemini key at all.
